analysis.title: US Economics Analyst: The Causes and Consequences of a Low-Hire, Low-Fire Labor Market
key_insights: The US labor market has settled into a low-hire, low-fire form of full employment, with hiring, quits and layoff rates all below pre-pandemic levels.
Low turnover is the main reason GS's ten-measure slack tracker signals a labor market somewhat softer than the unemployment rate alone suggests.
Job reallocation has fallen since the late 1990s but the decline has slowed. It sits just 0.2pp below its 2015-2019 average, so it contributes little to the recent turnover slowdown.
Churn, worker moves between existing jobs, explains most of the recent turnover decline and most variation since the early 2010s. It is almost 1pp below its 2015-2019 average.
Structural drivers of lower churn are an aging workforce and better worker-firm matching, but churn is still unusually low beyond these trends.
Two temporary factors are cited: post-pandemic normalization of job-switching, and an emerging AI effect. Churn has fallen further in industries with higher AI adoption and automation potential.

A GS labor market perception indicator has deteriorated sharply since last year despite a stable unemployment rate, with a sharper drop among young workers who are likely more exposed to AI displacement risk.

Reduced turnover modestly hurts job-finding. The job-finding rate has fallen more in industries and states with larger churn declines, and unemployment spells have lengthened roughly twice as much there. There is little evidence young workers are faring disproportionately worse.
Depressed churn is estimated to weigh on year-over-year wage growth by about 0.3pp. The GS wage tracker is slightly below 3.5%.
GS expects turnover to pick up somewhat as the temporary drags fade. If low turnover persists, it risks dampening productivity growth by hindering better worker-firm matches.
Some Fed officials, including Governor Waller and the October FOMC minutes, have highlighted unusually low labor market dynamism.
GS forecast table shows unemployment at 4.2% through 2027, core PCE at 2.4% in Q4 2027, and a Fed funds range of 4-4.25% at end 2027.

risk_factors: Persistently low turnover could lock out unemployed workers and lengthen unemployment spells.
Reduced dynamism could dampen productivity growth by hindering better worker-firm matches.
AI-related job insecurity may keep churn and wage growth depressed longer than expected.
The unemployment rate may overstate labor market health given depressed churn.
